text:
Treyvhon Saunders’ 2025 football season was shaping up to be one of the best in the entire FCS.

Through five games, he was the best receiver in the FCS with 50 receptions, 700 receiving yards, and six touchdowns. And then on Oct. 11, his senior season came to a screeching halt. He fractured his fibula on the Raiders’ first drive against Richmond.

“At first, there was definitely a lot of frustration,” Saunders said. “A lot of questioning why this happened to me. And I think my mind first went to not being able to play with my senior guys anymore, not being able to finish my senior year. Then it went to questioning, ‘What are my goals going to be like for the NFL?'”

Even though he was down, Saunders wasn’t out. Adversity is nothing new to him. He lost his mother in 2019 to ALS.

“Watching her pass in front of my eyes, and two hours before she passed, I was telling her about the NFL and how I was gonna make it,” Saunders said.

“He’s such a competitive person, and that’s how he was in rehab too,” Colgate head football coach Curt Fitzpatrick said. “Every day was a game day. He was setting mini goals for himself and competing with the process and just determined to get back so he could fulfill his dream of being a professional football player.”

Saunders never stopped working through his rehab and ended up recovering ahead of schedule, just in time for his pro day at Syracuse.

“He’s one of those kids that’s not gonna be denied,” his father, Scott Saunders, said. “To get to this stage where he’s working at that is incredible because it’s something that he had planned.”

Playing in the NFL has been his dream since he was five years old, and once Saunders walks into a building, he’ll be ready to make an impact and fulfill his dream.

“He’s got a unique ability to make other people better and push everyone around him,” Fitzpatrick said.

“My dreams can come true, and it’s right there, and I feel like I can reach out for it and grab it,” Treyvhon said. “It’s what I’ve been trying to do every single day, just put my head down and work as hard as I can because I know that there’s a moment where if my name gets called, or if I don’t, if I get called up, regardless of what it is, I know that I’ll be able to just look at myself and be proud of everything I overcame in these last few months and all the things that I overcame in my lifetime.”

Good news has been hard to come by for the Phillies lately, but this qualifies: Zack Wheeler is returning to the rotation this coming weekend. He'll take the mound Saturday against the first-place Braves with Bryce Elder as the opposing starter.

Wheeler had part of a rib removed during thoracic outlet decompression surgery this past offseason, a procedure that followed the discovery of a blood clot in the area of his right shoulder late last season. He made five minor-league rehab starts between Double-A and Triple-A.

"I think he's basically at the end of spring training," manager Rob Thomson said Tuesday (via MLB.com). "The fastball velocity's gone up. It's not where it's gonna be, I don't believe. The command has been some days good, some days not as good. But I'm expecting on a normal day, weather-wise, that he's gonna have his command.

"He's really spun the ball well during all of his outings, so I feel good about him."

Is Rob Thomson already on the hot seat? Why Phillies manager's job security could be dependent on the fans

Dayn Perry

In terms of the statistical results, Wheeler had a 5.85 ERA and 1.20 WHIP during his rehab assignment. Keep in mind that Thomson said it's basically like spring training, in that it's more important for the pitcher to get his work in and utilize all his pitchers instead of only focusing on preventing runs. In 20 innings, he struck out 23 and walked only five.

Still, Wheeler allowed four runs on six hits in four innings in Double-A last time out.

The big-league club is doing its share of struggling, too. The loss to the Cubs Tuesday night was the Phillies' seventh straight and they've dropped nine of their last 11 games. They've only scored 80 runs (3.47 per game), ranking 28th in the majors, ahead of only the Giants and Mets. The team ERA (4.99) also ranks 28th, ahead of only the Nationals and Astros.

Wheeler, before his blood clot, was arguably the most reliable ace in baseball. In his six years with the Phillies, he's 69-37 with a 2.91 ERA (146 ERA+), 1.02 WHIP and 1,094 strikeouts against 220 walks in 979 innings. He twice finished second in NL Cy Young voting and was tracking toward another top-two finish before going down last season.

text:
We’re nearly 24 hours from the start of the NFL draft, and we preview where the second-best quarterback could be headed. Plus, the NBA playoffs had an eventful night with a major star going down hard with an injury and all three underdogs taking Game 2.

NFL DRAFT:

One of the most interesting storylines of this year’s NFL draft is where Ty Simpson, who is the consensus second-ranked quarterback, will go.

After Fernando Mendoza goes first overall to the Las Vegas Raiders, there aren’t a ton of obvious landing spots for Simpson in the first round.

Even if Aaron Rodgers returns, the Pittsburgh Steelers jump out, but they’d have to really love him to take him top 25 (I don’t expect that). The New York Jets have their bridge quarterback in Geno Smith, and new offensive coordinator Frank Reich might prefer a bigger, more traditional pocket passer to develop. The earliest they’d most likely consider him is the first pick of the second round, but that’s not a lock at all.

That brings us to the Arizona Cardinals picking 34th overall (the second pick of Round 2). They have veterans Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew on the roster, but no one with long-term upside. Could Simpson make it to 34, or would things become even more interesting with Arizona moving into the back end of the first round, much like the Giants did for Jaxson Dart last year?

It’s a tale as old as time: the bright lights on a quarterback enduring a potential draft day fall. Rodgers went through it. More recently, Will Levis went through it. All eyes are on what’s next for Simpson.

NBA RECAP:

LeBron James turned back the clock one more time last night, putting up a very Jamesian stat line of 28 points, eight rebounds and seven assists in a 101-94 win over the Houston Rockets, giving the Los Angeles Lakers a 2-0 lead in their first-round series.

Thus far, the 41-year-old James has been able to control the pace of play against Houston. Though not quite at the same height athletically, James is playing very similarly to the player who once led his teams to eight straight NBA Finals appearances. He received a big boost from Marcus Smart and Luke Kennard in Game 2, as they combined for 48 points and shot 8-of-13 from 3.

Kevin Durant was held in check, scoring 23 points — and only 3 in the second half — in his return from a knee injury.

Los Angeles now takes a two-game lead to Houston despite missing both Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves.

“When we have two big guns out like we have, we’ve all got to pick up our play, and that’s all it’s about,” James said. “We’re all just trying to make contributions on offense and seize the opportunity.”

Earlier, the Philadelphia 76ers upset the Celtics in Boston, evening their series at 1-1 thanks to a dazzling performance by the duo of Tyrese Maxey and V.J. Edgecombe. Maxey scored 29, while Edgecombe had 30 points and 10 rebounds, becoming the youngest player in NBA history to post those numbers in the playoffs. He’s also the first rookie with a 30-10 game since Tim Duncan.

Philadelphia beat Boston at its own game, outscoring the Celtics from 3 by 18.

The Portland Trail Blazers also won a road Game 2, stealing home court from the San Antonio Spurs in a thrilling finish. Portland came back from down 14 in the fourth quarter to secure the victory. San Antonio was missing Victor Wembanyama for much of the night, as he left the game in the second quarter after a nasty fall led to a concussion. When Wemby will return is up in the air.

With the NFL draft taking over Pittsburgh, city officials described to NBC News why they decided to make kids go to remote learning for public schools.

Patriots coach Mike Vrabel made his first comments since the photo scandal with reporter Dianna Russini.

Did the New York Mets win last night? For the 12th straight game, the answer is no.

Columbus will be the 18th NWSL franchise, starting in 2028. The owners paid a record $205 million expansion fee.

Raiders Super Bowl legendRod Martin died. He was 72.

New Trail Blazers owner Tom Dundon doesn’t care that others say he’s cheap.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander won the NBA Clutch Player of the Year award.

The NFL has defended its streaming strategy to the Trump administration, an FCC filing shows.

Ice? Hardwood? The NBA and NHL playoffs both continue with big games tonight, with pivotal moments coming up in multiple series across both sports. text:
Jeff Zrebiec: 'It's Fair to Be Cautiously Optimistic' Nnamdi Madubuike Has Good Chance to Play in 2026

There was finally some news on Tuesday about one of the biggest questions of the Ravens' offseason, and it was encouraging.

Per ESPN’s Adam Schefter, two-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike, who suffered a season-ending neck injury in Week 2 last year, underwent neck surgery last week that left his doctors believing he will be able to resume playing in 2026.

Neither the Ravens nor Madubuike have commented on the report, but there had been indications of optimism over the past few months. On Jan. 30, Madubuike wrote "Good news" on social media, accompanied by a prayer hands emoji. He has also posted videos of himself working out.

While the report is indeed encouraging, The Athletic's Jeff Zrebiec said expectations should be tempered.

"It is good news that he continues to work towards playing, but let's proceed with caution," Zrebiec said on the “Baltimore Collective” podcast. "This doesn't mean he's going to return. My understanding is they still don't know. Yes, the surgery's probably necessary if he was going to have a shot to play, but it doesn't mean he's certainly going to play. They still don't really have a definitive timeline yet on it. We're talking about neck surgery. You don't know how he's going to react. You don't know how he's going to feel down the road, how he's going to respond to physicality, contact, all that stuff.

"Surgery doesn't mean Ravens doctors are going to green-light him to play. That's a major step. So, he has the surgery, that gives him a chance to play. We'll see how he recovers. We'll see how he continues to rehab. And then the Ravens doctors are going to have to make a decision here, assuming everything's going OK, whether they'll clear him to get back on a football field. So, we're nowhere near there yet. I would say it's not out of the woods yet, but I think it's fair to be cautiously optimistic that he has a good chance of playing this year."

If Madubuike does come back and is able to return to his pre-injury form, it obviously would be a huge boost for the defense. The unit was 24th in yards allowed last season and tied for the third-fewest sacks in the league.

Madubuike, 28, had a career-high 13 sacks in 2023 when he was named a second-team All-Pro and finished in the top 10 in Defensive Player of the Year voting. From the start of 2023 until he was placed on injured reserve, Madubuike's 21.5 sacks were the most among defensive tackles.

How Ravens Go About Predicting the Draft

General Manager Eric DeCosta noted at the Ravens' pre-draft press conference last week that the first couple rounds of the draft are "pretty easy to predict."

"There seems to be more of a consensus among teams," DeCosta said. "I think part of that is because of media coverage and social media and things like that, with consensus boards and different things that you can get online."

The Baltimore Banner’s Jonas Shaffer said the rise of predictive models among NFL teams such as the Ravens has also made the draft easier to forecast.

"In Baltimore, the Ravens' draft model seems to loom almost as large as their draft board itself," Shaffer wrote. "Team officials entered Day 2 [of the 2024 draft] hoping to draft an offensive tackle. Derrick Yam, the Ravens' director of data and decision science, told DeCosta there was an 80% chance Roger Rosengarten would be available late in the second round.

"DeCosta considered that an optimistic projection. Yam, DeCosta recalled, nervously conceded that the estimate could be off. But when the Ravens were on the clock again at No. 62 overall, Rosengarten was still available."

Shaffer said there's plenty of "educated guesswork" involved in preparing for the draft.

"In March, DeCosta said he signed outside linebacker Trey Hendrickson to a four-year, $112 million contract in part because he believed the pass rushers the Ravens would 'probably covet' in the draft would be unavailable by No. 14 overall," Shaffer wrote.

Ravens Fans Forced to Take Backseat to Steelers Fans at Draft

The Ravens-Steelers rivalry isn't confined to the field. It'll be on display during the draft in Pittsburgh, thanks to a move by Steelers Owner Art Rooney II after he looked at the seating chart for the event.

"I noticed that the Ravens fans were seated in front of the Steelers fans in one section of the draft theatre," Rooney said on a Pittsburgh radio station's morning show, per Steelers Depot’s Ross McCorkle. "So I asked [the NFL] to make that change, and they agreed."

Chalk it up to Pittsburgh having home-field advantage.

"With the draft returning to Pittsburgh on Thursday night, Ravens fans making the four-hour commute will be treated to the first players selected in the coach Jesse Minter era, and they'll get to watch while trying to see over the back of Steelers fans' heads," The Baltimore Sun’s Sam Cohn wrote.

The Ravens have never hosted the draft, but Ravens President Sashi Brown said last month that bringing the event to Baltimore remains a realistic goal.

"So maybe in the next few years, Ravens Owner Steve Bisciotti can settle the score and push Steelers fans to the back of the theater," Cohn wrote.

text:
The mood inside Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium after their Merseyside derby loss on Sunday was sombre.

Ashen-faced officials walked around in near silence as they attempted to come to terms with a crushing late defeat, sealed by Virgil van Dijk’s 100th-minute header, that damaged Everton’s hopes of European qualification.

The sight of an injured Jarrad Branthwaite limping through the media room on crutches, with his right leg in a brace, did little to improve the tone. Such measures are standard procedure for most injured players after matches, but the early prognosis on the 23-year-old defender had not been positive.

It was Branthwaite’s reaction to his 87th-minute injury that had caused most concern. He had been limping earlier in the second half, briefly dropping to the turf before attempting to continue, but later slid into the pitchside advertising hoardings after a challenge with Cody Gakpo and stayed down holding his hamstring.

After a lengthy pause for treatment, he was in tears and pulled his shirt over his face as he was taken off by stretcher. Everton manager David Moyes briefly consoled Branthwaite with an empathetic pat and some words of encouragement as he was taken down the tunnel.

Fans attempted to rally behind a key player, chanting “There’s only one Jarrad Branthwaite” as he was carried off the pitch. They and Moyes already know that far too well.

Branthwaite’s injury was not only a sobering setback for a player who has struggled with persistent fitness issues — mainly muscular — but also a significant blow to Everton’s dreams of playing in continental competition next season.

“We are worried,” Moyes said in his post-match press conference, before pointing out that further assessments would be needed to determine the precise extent and severity of Branthwaite’s latest problem.

Even at that early stage, the assumption was that his season, with only five games left, was almost certainly over. Most of the debate centred on whether this issue was as serious as the previous ones — also with his right hamstring — that led to him missing the first half of the campaign, and what that will mean for his pre-season schedule, given the importance of players taking part in a full programme.

Everton’s players and staff were off on Monday, as is usual on the day after a game, but Branthwaite went for a scan to assess the damage.

The results confirmed those fears that he probably won’t play in any of those remaining five fixtures, but there is more optimism now about his prospects of returning for pre-season, provided he encounters no setbacks during his rehabilitation. The general sense from those close to the situation is that the injury is not as bad as first feared.

Everton announced on Wednesday that no surgery would be needed this time, adding “the injury is unrelated to the hamstring area which required surgery in October”. They said Branthwaite was unlikely to feature again this season.

The injury ends Branthwaite’s hopes of making England’s World Cup squad for this summer’s tournament in North America. That was always a long shot, but he had been pushing for selection.

The possibility of him returning for Everton’s summer schedule has at least brought some relief after Sunday’s painful scenes, but the attention now turns to Branthwaite’s treatment, as well as the repercussions — short and long term — for both player and club.

For now, Everton have to find a way through the rest of their season without someone who is an important figure from a tactical standpoint. Nobody else in the back line has his pace, composure or left-footed ball-playing ability.

Branthwaite adds balance, allowing Everton to push higher up the pitch and be more aggressive in their play. He brings comfort to those around him, sweeping up attacks down the left flank. Both left-back Vitalii Mykolenko and regular captain James Tarkowski appear to play better when he is on the pitch with them. There is no perfect solution with Branthwaite missing.

Michael Keane, who is trusted by Moyes and has improved this season, is the most likely direct replacement. At 33, he brings different elements to the table — including, ironically, a finishing ability similar to that of a striker — and already knew Tarkowski well from their time together at Burnley. But Moyes will now need to tighten up his defensive setup to guard against balls in behind and issues in transition.

A further injury to Keane or Tarkowski would almost certainly prompt a reshuffle, with Jake O’Brien shifting inside to his favoured role and a new right-back coming in. Were that to be recent England debutant and versatile midfielder James Garner, that would mean another change in the centre of the park. The lack of a permanent, favoured right-back, together with injuries, means Everton’s defensive resources are thinly spread.

In the long term, Everton must reduce their exposure to such injuries. They are likely to look to retain Keane, who is seen as a steadying presence by Moyes, beyond the end of the season, when his current contract expires. That deal includes a club option for a further year, should Everton wish to trigger it, instead of negotiating fresh terms.

A new right-back will also be targeted in the summer transfer window. That would allow Republic of Ireland international O’Brien to return full time to central defence, which is where he sees his future, and give Moyes a fourth option at that position.

Everton have invested heavily in Branthwaite, rejecting the overtures of Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur, among others, in the past and signing him to a much-improved long-term contract last summer.

When The Friedkin Group completed its takeover in December 2024, the most likely scenario was that Branthwaite would be sold at the end of that season. But Moyes made the case that he wanted to build around Branthwaite, such is his talent. He is now one of Everton’s highest-paid players but has made just 10 Premier League appearances this season, seven of those starts.

Branthwaite struggled with thigh problems during previous manager Sean Dyche’s time in charge. But his recent issues have been hamstring-related and he has ended up locked in a cycle of injuries and setbacks. Everton tried to manage him carefully after his return to the squad in late January, keeping him out of certain games and training days, but that has not been enough.

In this new period, the focus will almost certainly be on getting to the bottom of what is going wrong and why. There are unlikely to be any easy answers.

Branthwaite’s tearful reaction at the weekend showed how heavily injuries can weigh on players — Premier League footballers are paid well but are still human. Being deprived of the ability to do what they love takes its toll.

He had returned to the side in fine form and was a standout performer in the derby before being forced off. Internally, there was a belief he was back to something approaching his best, making those dashed World Cup chances another bitter pill for him to swallow.

Branthwaite and Everton will now spend the next couple of months trying to find ways to end this cycle of misery.

text:
Unless there is a new rumor or move made, there is nothing new under the sun when it comes to the 2026 NFL draft. Until proven otherwise, despite a previous suggestion, many will assume that the Cleveland Browns are either drafting a wide receiver, an offensive tackle, and/or trading down in the first round of the draft.

We can mock draft in a million ways, including our more “win-now” version published on Wednesday morning, but the Browns will have to wait through a number of picks, with a shorter window between selections, to find out what GM Andrew Berry will do.

Given Berry’s NFL draft history, Cleveland fans are doubtful of this front office’s ability to make good decisions. In response to a big Myles Garrett trade package possibility, we saw this as the start of a response:

In no way do I trust the Browns in a draft.

That means, as this title indicates, fans are more likely to assume whoever Cleveland takes this year is the riskiest prospect to bust and whoever they pass over that they should have taken was the safest option. A look at the Top 25 prospects in the 2026 NFL draft, according to the Consensus Big Board, gives us this list:

QB Fernando Mendoza

LB Arvell Reese

Edge David Bailey

RB Jeremiyah Love

LB Sonny Styles

OT Francis Mauigoa

S Caleb Downs

WR Carnell Tate

Edge Rueben Bain

CB Mansoor Delane

OT Spencer Fano

WR Jordyn Tyson

WR Makai Lemon

OT Monroe Freeling

CB Jermod McCoy

iOL Olaivavega Ioane

TE Kenyon Sadiq

S Dillon Thieneman

OT Kadyn Proctor

Edge Keldric Faulk

Edge Akheem Mesidor

WR Omar Cooper Jr.

WR Kevin Concepcion

S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren

WR Denzel Boston

Trying to identify who is a risk and who is safe always starts with injuries. To some extent, those can’t be predicted, but there are indicators. Tyson, McCoy and Mauigoa have a history of concerns leading up to the NFL draft.

After injuries, where a player lands can often set them up for success or failure. Without any way to predict either injuries or landing spots, we are left with trying to just look at the prospects as they are.

Downs seems like the safest bet to be a very good player for a long time. After that, Love is the lone elite offensive prospect in this year’s group. On the risky side, Mendoza, as the first overall pick in a draft with no other top-level quarterbacks, could set him up for failure, while Reese’s tweener role at The Ohio State leaves room for the possibility of not reaching his potential in a specific role, and Bain’s short arms are historical outliers.

Proctor could be the biggest boom/bust prospect in the entire draft, with a chance to be a Top 5 left tackle or out of the league too soon (Alabama’s OLine history is very concerning).

For the Browns, the team needs talented players, but playing it safe could keep them from getting an elite prospect. There is never a right answer for a team that is trying to find its winning ways. If a safe pick is just good, not great, the upside is limited. If a risky pick busts, it is a waste of an opportunity.

Who do you think is the safest pick among the top prospects in this year’s draft? Who do you think is the riskiest? Which way should the Browns lean in this year’s draft?

title: My favorite Day 3 NFL Draft guys for the Bengals this year
description:
Fortunately for the Bengals, they have five Day 3 picks to use to bolster their offensive line depth.
Even after the Lawrence trade, the Bengals will use a lot of their early draft capital on defense.
Offensive line could be the focus of the day on Day 3, and the Bengals need to come out of the draft with multiple offensive linemen (they also might need to sign an additional veteran).

1 overall pick Russell Maryland (a defensive tackle).
text:
Ted Karras is one of the most optimistic people you’ll ever meet, and he’s as excited as anyone about the moves the Cincinnati Bengals have made this offseason.

“We’re a little bit light on O-Line numbers wise,” Karras said on Monday as he surveyed the Bengals’ roster after the Dexter Lawrence trade. “We’ll see if we have some nice additions and go get as good as we can this spring.”

Until Karras said it, I didn’t realize just how “light” the Bengals were.

The starting five is the best it has been in the Burrow era. Cody Ford and Jalen Rivers, who profile best as backup guards who can flex out to tackle in a true emergency situation, are the only other backups on the team with names that you’d recognize. We’ll see if Andrew Coker, Javon Foster and Jacob Bayer can turn any heads in training camp, but those aren’t guys who you go into camp with expecting to be on your roster.

Fortunately for the Bengals, they have five Day 3 picks to use to bolster their offensive line depth.

Even after the Lawrence trade, the Bengals will use a lot of their early draft capital on defense. One of the defining strategic questions of the draft for the Bengals will be how long they feel like they can wait for a swing tackle. That’s a glaring, red-flag need, and you don’t want to go in the season with a true backup guard (Ford/Rivers) being a snap away from playing tackle.

Offensive line could be the focus of the day on Day 3, and the Bengals need to come out of the draft with multiple offensive linemen (they also might need to sign an additional veteran). They could also look for a receiver to complement Mitchell Tinsley and develop in the background (in the Andrei Iosivas mold). The tight ends are interesting. And if there’s a defensive player who you like on Day 3, you’ll be able to find a role for him on a Bengals’ defense that still doesn’t have much depth at edge (Isaiah Foskey is DE5), linebacker (Shaka Hayward is LB4) or safety (PJ Jules is S4).

The Bengals don’t have a fifth-round pick but have two sixths and two sevenths.

Round 4 favorites

Miami OT Markell Bell. If you could guarantee now that Bell will be on the board in Round 4, that would probably give the Bengals a lot of reassurance. The best case scenario for this draft feels like defense in Rounds 2 and 3 and Bell in Round 4. He’s the classic big Bengals tackle, he didn’t allow a sack last year and he’s a winner.

Boston College OT Jude Bowry. A college captain who has the athleticism to be versatile and the size to set up shop at tackle. He has raw athletic tools to develop and size to play a role right away.

Oklahoma OL Febechi Nwaiwu. He has experience all across the line, Dane Brugler touted him as having some of the highest character in the draft and he’s a pass pro oriented player who can handle the power of the AFC North. He doesn’t cover a ton of ground, but he’s long and packs a punch. The Bengals reportedly showed plenty of interest during the pre-draft process.

Michigan OLB Jimmy Rolder. He’s a balanced athlete and a bit of a jack of all trades as a guy who can mix it up in the box or run around the field to chase a ball carrier. He has real athletic upside that he’s just tapping into, but he does need to clean up his tackling. He profiles as the combo linebacker/edge that they’re looking for, and he’d come at a bargain with the Bengals using a fourth-rounder there instead of a second-round pick.

Ohio State edge Caden Curry. While he was a very productive pass rusher in college, he projects in the NFL as a physical, tone setting defensive end who’s perfectly fine running full speed into tackles 50 times a game to seal off run lanes. The measurables aren’t great, but he’s physical. I also have a soft spot for defensive players who were used as fullbacks.

Oregon WR Malik Benson. My favorite Day 3 receiver. He runs downfield all day, tracks the ball incredibly well and was a big play machine. He might be more limited to just vertical routes, but he’s very good at them and would punish teams that leave him one-on-one against a No. 3 corner. Keep in mind as you’re scouting receivers that the Bengals hate guys who drop passes — Benson doesn’t. He also offers punt return value.

Florida corner Devin Moore. A sticky cover corner with the size, length and consistent tape that you’re looking for. He just has a very long injury history, missing half of the season in three of his four years of college.

Round 6 favorites

Florida LB George Gumbs. From walk-on wide receiver in the MAC to a five-sack defensive end in the SEC, Gumbs has one of the best stories in this class. Some view him as an undersized edge, but his background and his current physical frame suggest that Gumbs might be a better fit at linebacker. He looks like one, and the power, physicality, effort and ability to drop in coverage that he showed as a defensive end at Florida would all help him translate at linebacker. He can also help on special teams.

Arkansas guard Fernando Carmona. A versatile captain from the SEC with reps and experience who’s known for his anchor and ability in pass pro. Sounds like a Bengal.

Michigan State center/guard Matt Gulbin. He has a similar profile with the added ability to snap, which the Bengals need. In the transfer portal era, I’m really impressed with players who change schools and become a captain right away. His profile suggests that he’s a jack of all trades, master of none. He may be a long-term sixth man/backup on your line, but that’s a nice outcome for a sixth-round pick.

Wyoming guard Caden Barnett. He’s the best wrestler in this draft, which highlights some of his tools. He’ll have to make the small school jump, but his frame, aggressive style, ability to hold up against power and strength feels Cordell Volson-esque. That would be a successful outcome here.

Baylor WR Josh Cameron. A physical contested catch winner with traits worth betting on. He’s not a burner, but he can make the plays that Mitchell Tinsley did last year with his impressive strength, leap and terrific hands. He’s also a captain who returns punts.

Cincinnati WR Jeff Caldwell. The prototypical traits-based sixth-round receiver with elite height and speed combination.

Ole Miss TE Dae’Quan Wright. My favorite tight end in the draft. He generates splash plays, gets downfield for catches in the deep and intermediate passing game and was a focal point of his college offense. He’s a receiver-first tight end and would fit the Bengals in that way. He was versatile enough to line up in different spots, and he ranked second in the country in yards per catch. Dane Brugler also noted his improvements and toughness as a blocker.

USC edge Anthony Lucas. A five-star recruit who didn’t live up to expectations in college but is still relatively inexperienced as he got a late start to football. His traits, size, length and strength alone give him the ability to set the edge.

Round 7 favorites

Georgia guard Micah Morris. He was Dylan Fairchild’s backup and then took over that spot. He had to wait his turn on a stacked Georgia line, which cost him some reps and development. But he had the strength, power and potential to be in that mix in the first place.

Indiana center Pat Coogan. You’ve got to be smart to play center for the Bengals, and Coogan’s intangibles shined last year. Al Golden was with him for a few years at Notre Dame. He’s not the traitsiest, most nimble interior offensive lineman. But he’s tough, smart and has experience at guard. He has the raw size but is missing some length. Still, his track record said that he should have a chance to stick as a backup.

Nebraska safety/hybrid DB DeShon Singleton. His impressive combination of frame and athleticism instantly give him the look of an impact special teamer. As a team captain at Nebraska, he made a ton of plays in coverage on the ball, which is intriguing as well. Reports say that he also held his own in the slot, especially against tight ends. He feels like a guy who gives you depth in different spots and makes a career on special teams.

SMU tight end RJ Maryland. Remarkably fast. Son of former No. 1 overall pick Russell Maryland (a defensive tackle). Torn ACL in 2024 took away at his shot at a big breakout season in 2025, but his testing numbers showed a rare smooth athleticism for his position. Great down the seam, which would add something new to the Bengals. He also got plenty of snaps last year in the slot, which suggests an interesting potential to be a big, fast power slot who could make plays down the field and also make a big impact on special teams (like NFL veteran Ben Skowronek). Could provide a fun schematic wrinkle.

title: If Mystery Was Plan, Cardinals In Good Spot Going Into NFL Draft
description:
How the Cardinals judge their 2026 draft won't be known for a few years.
But their work ahead of the draft, at least in terms of shrouding it in mystery, has been impressive.
Many analysts believe the best player in the draft is Love.
"I have no idea where I'm going, but there's a lot of talk of me going to the Titans, Cardinals, Giants," Love said.
Would the Cardinals trade back into the late second round to get him and take a chance at finding the quarterback of the future?
text:
How the Cardinals judge their 2026 draft won't be known for a few years.

But their work ahead of the draft, at least in terms of shrouding it in mystery, has been impressive.

When the Cardinals are on the clock at No. 3 on Thursday night, the uncertainty – looking from the outside – is thick. Sure, a trade down is possible, but finding a partner was always going to be the issue. Cases can be made for either David Bailey or Arvell Reese as an edge rusher, or an offensive lineman like Francis Mauigoa, or even talented running back Jeremiyah Love.

Unlike 2024, when the Cardinals were choosing fourth and the selection of wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. seemed inevitable, this year's first round has a much different feel.

"The thing (coach) Mike (LaFleur) and I have talked about is we can never go wrong taking who we feel is the best player, who fits this team, (and) who is about what we're about," general manager Monti Ossenfort said. "When someone can check those boxes, we're going to be happy with that player, whatever position they're playing."

The key phrase there is "who fits this team." That addendum changes the equation.

Many analysts believe the best player in the draft is Love. The Cardinals signed Tyler Allgeier in free agency, they kept James Conner, they still have Trey Benson. And they have needs for a dynamic pass rusher and a right tackle.

When LaFleur was asked about taking a running back early – a Love question without a Love mention – the first-year head coach wasn't ruling anything out.

"I like what you're alluding to right there," LaFleur said. "I know I'm going to give you the political answer, but it's the truth. You just want to draft the best football player that's going to fit your team and what you're looking for, regardless of the position."

Love was asked by reporters in Pittsburgh on Wednesday about his potential future employer.

"I have no idea where I'm going, but there's a lot of talk of me going to the Titans, Cardinals, Giants," Love said. "Honestly, I'd be blessed to go anywhere."

Who the pick is at 3 is only one storyline the Cardinals are living in the moment. The trade, if someone wants to come up to 3 for an edge or Love, can't be ignored. What teams might be offering, however, will be the key in a draft that offers no real sexy reason (i.e. quarterback) to move up.

Then there is the Ty Simpson discussion. No one believes the Cardinals would take the Alabama quarterback at 3. But would he last until No. 34, the Cardinals' second-round choice, the second pick of the second round? Would the Cardinals trade back into the late second round to get him and take a chance at finding the quarterback of the future?

Even if the team stays at 3 and makes a choice by 5:30 p.m. Arizona time, the drama surrounding the team won't go away as the first round progresses.

The Cardinals have seven total picks. Regardless of when, getting an off-ball linebacker, an offensive lineman or two, a quarterback and another defensive lineman wouldn't be a surprise.

But the equation changes as names come off the board too, as does the lens through which the Cardinals see their needs.

"You can't just look at it like, 'Hey, how's this going to affect us tomorrow and the next day?'" Ossenfort said. "Every decision affects every decision moving forward. Our goal is to put as competitive of a team as we can to go into '26 and go 1-0 every week. That's what we're trying to do with the realization every decision we make affects subsequent years.

"I don't think those are two independent thoughts."

text:
PITTSBURGH -- NFL teams received a letter Wednesday about the progress of former Florida defensive tackle Caleb Banks as he recovers from a surgically repaired bone in his left foot.

The letter states that Banks underwent a CT scan Tuesday and is "on pace to be fully cleared for full football activities in early June," sources told ESPN.

The letter and timeline come after Dr. Norman Waldrop, a foot and ankle specialist with the Andrews Clinic, looked at Banks' scan. Banks had surgery March 9 on a fractured fourth metatarsal of his left foot.

Banks is among the top defensive tackles in this year's draft class, and a strong showing at the Senior Bowl in January bolstered his draft stock. But he suffered a broken bone in his foot at the NFL scouting combine in February, raising questions about his health after Banks played in just three games during the 2025 season at Florida because of an injury to the same foot.

Banks, who is 6-foot-6 and 327 pounds, is ranked among the top five defensive tackles in all of ESPN's draft analyst ratings. Both Jordan Reid and Field Yates rank him No. 3 at the position.

In 2024, Banks proved to be a dominant interior player in the SEC, finishing with seven tackles for loss, 4.5 sacks and two forced fumbles, and he entered the 2025 season as a second-team All-SEC preseason selection.

He played 12 games at Florida in both 2023 and 2024, logging 19 tackles and 1.5 tackles for loss in 2023.
